title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 33
paragraphs: When all had been drawn up by nations and divisions, on the next day they offered sacrifice on both sides. For the Greeks, Tisamenos son of Antiochos was the one who sacrificed, since he accompanied the army as diviner. This man the Lacedaemonians had made one of their own citizens, being an Eleian of the race of the Iamidai. For when Tisamenos was seeking divination at Delphi concerning issue, the Pythian priestess answered him that he should win five of the greatest contests. Missing the oracle's meaning, he turned to athletic games, supposing he would win athletic contests; he practiced for the pentathlon and came within a single fall of winning an Olympic victory, being matched against Hieronymos of Andros. But the Lacedaemonians perceived that the oracle given to Tisamenos referred not to athletic but to martial contests, and they tried to persuade Tisamenos by payment of money to become a leader in their wars alongside the kings of the house of Heracles. He, seeing that the Spartans set much store on gaining him as a friend, raised his price and made clear that he would do what they wanted only if they made him a citizen of their state with full rights — but for no other payment. At first the Spartans, hearing this, displayed indignation and gave up their request altogether; but at last, when great fear of this Persian armament hung over them, they gave in and agreed. He, perceiving they had changed their minds, then said that even so he could not now be satisfied with these terms alone: it was also necessary that his brother Hegias be made a Spartan citizen on the same terms as himself.
